overview.body: ENHANCE unit. Two big wins land together. First, hazards move out of lab-4-2.py and into hazards.txt, loaded into a list of dictionaries with a third loader function. Second, .upper() finally arrives. A new clean_input() helper strips whitespace and uppercases the result, collapsing every y/Y/n/N comparison into a single Y/N check. get_valid_int also gets smarter, using .isdigit() so typing abc at a numeric prompt no longer crashes the program. Two Patch Notes Tyler dropped back in Module 2 finally close this unit.

mentorQuote.quote: The player should never lose to bad input. They typed y instead of Y, the game crashed, they reload, they're annoyed. That's a design failure, not a player failure. clean_input() means we accept whatever the player types, uppercase, lowercase, with a stray space, and meet them where they are. That's what good interfaces feel like: invisible.

objectives: Rewrite get_valid_int in the library to use .isdigit() so non-numeric input is caught with a friendly error message instead of crashing with ValueError (closes Tyler's Patch Note from Lab 2-3, CP3)
Rewrite get_yes_no in the library to use clean_input. The 4-way 'y'/'Y'/'n'/'N' comparison collapses to a single Y/N check
Add load_hazards(filename) to the library, parsing hazards.txt into a list of dictionaries (closes Tyler's Patch Note from Lab 2-2, CP6)
Add handle_hazard(hazards) to the library: picks a random hazard, prints the encounter, flips the escape coin, returns a tuple (name, escaped)

In lab-4-2.py: copy 4.1 forward, delete the inline hazard parallel lists, load hazards.txt at startup, replace the inline hazard block in the travel loop with a single handle_hazard call, and retire get_random_hazard entirely
overview.keyConceptsText: .upper() and .strip() compose elegantly. input(prompt).strip().upper() reads from the user, removes any surrounding whitespace, and converts the result to uppercase, all in one expression. Wrapping that pattern in clean_input() means every input cleanup in the game looks the same. .isdigit() checks whether a string consists entirely of decimal digits, which is the right test for 'is this a non-negative whole number?' before calling int(). List of dictionaries is the third dictionary shape you've seen this module: a list whose items happen to be dicts. random.choice(hazards) returns one of those dicts, and hazard['name'] retrieves a field.

content.body: A rewrite of get_valid_int that checks the input with .isdigit() before converting it. Typing abc, 3.5, or nothing at all now gets a friendly error and a second chance instead of a crash.
Tyler flagged this gap back in Lab 2.3, CP3: the original function caught out-of-range numbers but crashed on anything that was not a number. .isdigit() arrives with Chapter 8, so the gap closes now.

content.quote: I have been waiting on this one. Back in 2-3 we agreed the function caught out-of-range numbers but would faceplant on abc or an empty string. The fix is .isdigit() from Chapter 8. Two lines of logic and the function stops crashing.

items: In function_library.py, rewrite get_valid_int(prompt, min_val, max_val). Start with valid = False and value = 0, then loop while not valid:.
Inside the loop, read and trim: user_input = input(prompt).strip().

If user_input.isdigit(): convert with value = int(user_input). If it is in range, set valid = True; otherwise print your existing out-of-range message, unchanged: f'ERROR: Enter a number between {min_val} and {max_val}.' At this depth it runs past 79 characters, so split it the way Python allows adjacent f-strings: print(f'ERROR: Enter a number between ' on one line and f'{min_val} and {max_val}.') on the next.
.isdigit() is False for negative numbers. Add elif user_input.startswith('-') and user_input[1:].isdigit(): and handle it the same way: convert, then range-check.
Otherwise, print('ERROR: Please enter a valid whole number.').
After the loop, return value. Update the docstring to say non-numeric input is rejected.

references.description: Demonstrates .isdigit(), .isalpha(), and friends. .isdigit() answers 'is this a whole number?'

Rewrite get_yes_no(prompt): answer = clean_input(prompt), then while answer != 'Y' and answer != 'N': print your existing message, unchanged, print("ERROR: Please enter 'y' or 'n'."), and ask again with answer = clean_input(prompt).
After the loop, return answer == 'Y': one comparison instead of two. Update the docstring.

ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: Check CP2 (Hazards From a File). The data file must be in the same folder as lab-4-2.py. CodeGrade provides it as a fixture. If the files ARE in the folder and it still fails, you almost certainly opened the FILE in VS Code instead of the FOLDER. Python then looks for the data files wherever VS Code was launched from, not next to your code. Use File → Open Folder and pick the lab folder itself; you should see the .txt files listed in the sidebar. Also keep them as plain .txt data files. Do not re-save them as .py.
Check CP3. The hazard block in the in-game loop still calls the old function. Replace it with the new handle_hazard call.

ifSomethingBreaks.symptom: ValueError: invalid literal for int() at a menu prompt
ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: Check CP4 (Number Input That Never Crashes). The .isdigit() rewrite did not land in the library, or the wrong version of function_library.py is being used.

ifSomethingBreaks.symptom: Yes/no prompt accepts y but rejects Y (or vice versa)
ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: Check CP5 (Clean Yes/No Answers). The rewrite uses clean_input, which uppercases its input, so the comparison should be against 'Y' and 'N' only.

ifSomethingBreaks.symptom: Trip report's HAZARDS section shows pairs like ("Buc-ee's appears!", True)
ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: Check CP3. The code appends the whole (name, escaped) pair. Append just name.

ifSomethingBreaks.symptom: Hazard prints fire but the trip report shows 0 hazards faced
ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: Check CP3. The hazards_faced = hazards_faced + 1 line is missing from the hazard block, or it sits outside the if where it never runs. (If Hazards Escaped is the wrong number instead, check the if escaped: line.)

ifYouGetStuck: Re-read Programs 8–6 (.upper()) and 8–7 (.isdigit()) before you start CP4 and CP5. These two BookEx programs are exactly the pattern you need
If you get FileNotFoundError for hazards.txt at startup, the file is not in the same folder as lab-4-2.py

If hazards print but the trip report shows none, check the unpacking: name, escaped = ( / function_library.handle_hazard(hazards)), the two-line form from CP3. Without name, escaped =, the return value is thrown away
